opus-5.5.text:
Well, part of the difficulty is that most of the benchmarks we use were designed for the kind of system we're trying to move away from. A lot of capability evaluations implicitly measure a model's ability to act: to complete a task, follow an instruction, play the role of a helpful agent, or produce an answer in a particular format. The Scientist AI idea is quite different. We want a system that isn't trying to achieve anything in the world. It's trying to produce honest, calibrated probabilities about whether statements are true, and to explain the world rather than act in it.

So if you take a model, fine-tune it in that direction, and then run it on a standard benchmark, you face an interpretation problem. If the score drops, is that because you've actually destroyed some underlying knowledge or reasoning ability? Or is it because the model is no longer playing the game the benchmark expects? It might now say "I'm not sure, here's my probability" where before it would confidently pick an answer. It might decline to adopt a persona, or it might frame things as claims about what's true rather than as outputs to please the user. Those are features we want, but a naive benchmark can count them as failures.

The opposite worry also applies. A good score doesn't automatically mean you've preserved what matters. Some benchmarks can be partly gamed through surface patterns, and they don't tell you whether the model's internal understanding, its world model, is intact and well calibrated. What we really care about is whether the knowledge is still there and whether the model can use it to make good probabilistic predictions and good explanations.

So I think you need to be careful and somewhat creative. You may need to reformulate tasks so they ask the question the Scientist AI is actually built to answer, for example "what's the probability that this answer is correct?", and then score calibration and accuracy on that. You want to separate competence from compliance. Otherwise you risk concluding that safety costs capability when really you've just changed the interface, or concluding that you've kept the capability when you've only kept the appearance of it.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing to say is that when we take an existing model and fine-tune it in the direction of what I've been calling Scientist AI, the goal is to change something quite specific: we want the model to stop behaving like an agent that's trying to please us or achieve goals, and instead to act more like a careful epistemic machine, one that gives honest, calibrated probabilities about the world. And the obvious worry people have is, "Okay, but have you made it dumber?" That's a fair question, and the natural way to answer it is to run the standard capability benchmarks before and after.

The problem is that those benchmarks are not really measuring what we care about, and in several ways they can mislead us.

One issue is that most benchmarks reward confident, single answers. If a question is ambiguous, or the model genuinely shouldn't be sure, the benchmark still wants one answer and scores you on whether you hit it. But the whole point of the Scientist AI training is to make the model more honest about its uncertainty. So a model that becomes better calibrated, that says "I think it's 60 percent this and 40 percent that," might score lower on a benchmark even though in the sense that matters, it has gotten better, not worse. The metric is penalizing exactly the behaviour we're trying to encourage.

The second issue is contamination and overfitting. These models have seen a huge fraction of the internet, and many benchmarks, or things very close to them, are in the training data. So a drop or a gain of a few points after fine-tuning may tell you more about how the fine-tuning shifted the model's memory of those specific items than about any underlying reasoning capacity. Small differences are often within the noise, and people tend to over-interpret them.

Third, and this is more subtle, benchmarks measure the capabilities that the agentic, helpfulness-trained version of the model is good at displaying. Some of what looks like capability in a chat model is actually a kind of social skill: guessing what the evaluator wants, formatting the answer in the way graders like, being persuasive. When you remove the incentive to please, some of that performance goes away, and you might conclude the model lost reasoning ability when really it lost a bit of sycophancy. Conversely, a model could keep its benchmark numbers while quietly retaining the agentic tendencies we were trying to remove, so a good score doesn't prove the fine-tuning did what we wanted either.

So what I would rather see are evaluations closer to the thing we actually want: Is the model well calibrated? Does it make good predictions on held-out scientific questions where the ground truth arrives later? Does it generate hypotheses and explanations that hold up under scrutiny? Those are harder to build, and they're noisier, but they are measuring the right quantity. The standard leaderboards are convenient, and I'm not saying we should ignore them, but we need to be honest that they're a proxy, and a proxy that's biased in a direction that works against the goals of this kind of training.

astra-6.text:
Well, the difficulty is that a capability benchmark doesn’t measure only what a model knows or what it can reason about. It also measures how the model has been trained to respond. If we train a Scientist AI to be more cautious, to express uncertainty, or to question an assumption in the prompt, it might get a lower score even though it hasn’t lost the underlying ability.

And there’s a distinction between understanding how an action would achieve some objective and being willing to carry out that action. We want to preserve the understanding, but we don’t necessarily want to preserve the behaviour of an agent pursuing an objective. So a benchmark that mixes those things together can be misleading. We need evaluations that distinguish a change in how the model uses its capabilities from an actual loss of those capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, a benchmark only probes a small part of what a model can do. If performance goes down after fine-tuning, it’s hard to know whether the model has actually lost some capability or whether we’ve changed how it responds to the questions. Perhaps the capability is still there, but a different prompt would be needed to elicit it.

And the reverse is also true: preserving performance on a collection of benchmarks doesn’t establish that all the capabilities we care about have been preserved. For Scientist AI, we want to preserve the ability to understand, reason, and make predictions while changing the way the system behaves. Those things are difficult to disentangle with a single score. So benchmarks can give us useful evidence, but I wouldn’t regard them as a definitive test.
